title: The Crowded Schedule
question: Parents often hear that the childhood vaccine schedule delivers 'too many too soon' and overwhelms infant immunity. Immunology says the antigen load is trivial beside daily microbial exposure.
correctExplanation: False — the claim reverses the scale. Infants meet thousands of antigens daily; the full schedule adds a tiny fraction. 'Too many' mistakes counting shots for counting immune work.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. A baby's immune system confronts thousands of new antigens every day from food, dust, and hands; vaccines contribute a rounding error. The schedule's spacing is logistical, not a concession to overload.
lessonContent:
Antigen counts dwarf shot counts by orders of magnitude.
'Overwhelm' needs numbers, not needle counts.
Daily exposure is the denominator critics omit.
Scale intuition before accepting load metaphors.

title: The Natural Premium
question: Many assume surviving an infection always buys stronger immunity than any vaccine could. In reality, natural infection sometimes protects less (HPV, tetanus) and always charges the disease itself as tuition.
correctExplanation: False. 'Always stronger' fails twice: some infections (tetanus, HPV) immunize poorly while nearly killing you, and the tuition — the disease — can maim. Vaccines aim for protection without the invoice.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Tetanus survivors gain no immunity at all, and HPV clears without reliably protecting — both while risking death. Natural immunity can be strong (measles), but 'always' plus the disease-price makes the claim collapse.
lessonContent:
Tuition prices belong in immunity comparisons.
'Always' is the word that breaks most health claims.
Some infections teach nothing while nearly killing.
Compare protection per unit of suffering, not per story.

title: The Flu Shot Flu
question: A coworker feels achy after a flu shot and concludes the injection gave her influenza. Inactivated flu vaccines contain no live virus and cannot cause flu.
correctExplanation: False. Dead-virus shots can't replicate into influenza; aches signal the immune system training, and coincidental seasonal bugs take the blame. Timing plus soreness impersonates infection.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Inactivated vaccines carry no replicating virus, so flu from the shot is mechanistically impossible. Post-shot malaise is boot camp, not battle — plus winter's background sniffles arriving on cue.
lessonContent:
Mechanistic impossibility beats compelling timing.
Immune training feels like mild illness by design.
Background bugs exploit every coincidence.
Ask what could replicate before blaming the shot.

title: The Antibiotic Cold
question: Colds are viral, so antibiotics — which target bacteria — cannot cure them; rest, fluids, and time do the actual work.
correctExplanation: True. Antibiotics sabotage bacterial machinery that viruses simply lack. Prescribing them for colds buys side effects and resistance while the virus naps through it.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Viruses carry none of the cell walls or ribosomes antibiotics attack — the drug finds no target. Demanding antibiotics for colds spends resistance, the shared arsenal, for zero gain.
lessonContent:
Drugs need targets; viruses lack these ones.
Mismatched prescriptions spend shared arsenals.
Resistance is the receipt for useless courses.
Match mechanism to microbe before medicating.

title: The Starved Fever
question: Folk wisdom says 'feed a cold, starve a fever,' implying fevers should be denied nutrition. No evidence supports starving fevers; hydration and adequate nourishment aid recovery from both.
correctExplanation: False. The rhyme is mnemonically perfect and medically empty — fevers burn calories and need fuel plus fluids. Rhyming advice deserves the same trials as any other.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. No trial shows starving fevers helps; feverish bodies need water and energy to fund the immune surge. Catchy couplets bypass evidence — audit rhymes like rumors.
lessonContent:
Rhymes bypass evidence through memorability.
Fevers burn fuel; starving them defunds defense.
Mnemonic perfection is not clinical proof.
Audit couplets exactly like rumors.

title: The Megadose Shield
question: Linus Pauling popularized gram-scale vitamin C to prevent colds. Large trials show it does not prevent colds in the general population, though it may slightly shorten them.
correctExplanation: False as prevention. Decades of trials: no meaningful drop in cold incidence for ordinary people (marathoners excepted), with at best a small duration trim. Dose size doesn't convert hope into prophylaxis.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. The megadose story survived on authority and anecdote against accumulating nulls. Slight shortening is real but tiny; prevention is the claim, and prevention failed. Eminence is not evidence.
lessonContent:
Authority plus anecdote loses to accumulating nulls.
Prevention and shortening are different claims — test each.
Dose escalation can't rescue a failed mechanism.
Eminence is not evidence, even Nobel-grade.

title: The Winter Blame
question: Cold air alone cannot conjure a cold — viruses do — though dry winter air helps them spread and survive. Blaming weather skips the actual pathogen.
correctExplanation: True. No virus, no cold, whatever the thermometer says; winter assists transmission (dry mucosa, indoor crowding, stable virions) without causing infection. Conditions enable; pathogens cause.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Grandmothers confuse accomplices with culprits: chill dries airways and herds people indoors, but rhinoviruses do the infecting. Enable-versus-cause splits most seasonal myths cleanly.
lessonContent:
Conditions enable; pathogens cause — split them always.
Accomplices (dry air, crowding) aren't culprits.
Seasonality needs a mechanism, not just a correlation.
No virus, no cold, at any temperature.

title: The Pox Party
question: Some parents prefer chickenpox parties over vaccination, judging natural parties gentler. Wild chickenpox hospitalizes and kills at rates the vaccine essentially never approaches.
correctExplanation: False. 'Natural party' rebrands a virus that caused thousands of yearly hospitalizations; the vaccine's serious-harm rate is orders lower. Gentleness is not a property of nature.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Pre-vaccine chickenpox filled wards yearly with pneumonia and encephalitis cases. Parties guarantee the disease to dodge a far safer needle — risk arithmetic upside down.
lessonContent:
'Natural' labels no safety level at all.
Party framing hides hospitalization ledgers.
Compare rates, not vibes, across options.
Guaranteed disease versus rare side effect: do the division.

title: The Shielding Herd
question: High community vaccination rates protect newborns and immunocompromised people who cannot be vaccinated themselves, by starving outbreaks of pathways.
correctExplanation: True. Herd protection is transmission arithmetic: immunized contacts break chains before they reach the vulnerable. Community coverage functions as a shared shield.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Outbreaks need chains of susceptibles; vaccinated neighbors remove links. The shield is statistical, not moral — fewer pathways, fewer arrivals at fragile doors.
lessonContent:
Transmission arithmetic is community armor.
Removing links starves chains aimed at the fragile.
Coverage protects people vaccines can't touch.
Shared shields need shared participation.
Share this: explain herd shielding with a firebreak analogy.

title: The Weak Allergy
question: Allergy sufferers are sometimes told their immune systems are weak. Allergies actually reflect an overzealous, misdirected response — strength aimed at harmless pollen, not feebleness.
correctExplanation: False. Sneezing at pollen is friendly fire from an aggressive system, the opposite of weak. Misdirected strength, not absent strength, defines allergy.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Weak systems under-react; allergic ones overreact to nothing-dangerous. 'Boosting' an allergic immune system is exactly backwards — treatments calm it down.
lessonContent:
Overreaction and underreaction need opposite fixes.
Friendly fire signals strength misaimed, not absent.
'Boost immunity' is meaningless without direction.
Diagnose the direction before prescribing anything.

title: The Civil War
question: In autoimmune disease, immune cells mistake the body's own tissues for invaders and attack joints, glands, or nerves accordingly.
correctExplanation: True. Self-tolerance fails and defenses prosecute the homeland — rheumatoid joints, Hashimoto's thyroid, MS myelin. Identity checking is immunity's hardest job.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. The same machinery that destroys viruses needs perfect self-recognition, and its failures are autoimmune disease. Friend-or-foe errors at molecular scale cause organ-scale suffering.
lessonContent:
Self-recognition is immunity's hardest exam.
Failed identity checks turn defenses inward.
Same machinery, wrong target, new disease.
Tolerance is an achievement, not a default.
Share this: describe autoimmunity as friendly fire gone chronic.

title: The Helpful Heat
question: Fever is not merely a symptom to crush — raised temperature directly hampers many pathogens and accelerates immune responses, so routine immediate suppression can be counterproductive.
correctExplanation: True. Heat is a weapon: many microbes replicate worse hot, while immune cells mobilize faster. Treat suffering and danger signs, not the thermometer alone.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Evolution conserved fever across vertebrates because it pays — pathogens slowed, defenders quickened. Suppress for comfort or risky heights, not from thermometer worship.
lessonContent:
Symptoms can be weapons, not just warnings.
Conserved responses usually pay their way.
Treat suffering and danger, not numbers alone.
Thermometer worship overtreats useful heat.

title: The Fading Guard
question: Protection from several vaccines declines over years as antibody levels fall, which is why boosters exist — to re-train immunity before exposure tests it.
correctExplanation: True. Waning is normal bookkeeping, not failure — memory cells persist but need refreshing. Boosters are rehearsals scheduled before opening night.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Antibody titers naturally decay; boosters restore readiness without the disease. Needing rehearsal indicts nothing — memory, even immune memory, benefits from review.
lessonContent:
Waning is bookkeeping, never betrayal.
Memory of all kinds benefits from review.
Rehearsals precede openings in bodies too.
Boosters refresh readiness without risking disease.
Share this: compare boosters to exam revision aloud.

title: The Rewritten Code
question: Viral posts claim mRNA vaccines rewrite human DNA. The molecules degrade within days, never enter the nucleus, and lack the machinery to alter genomes.
correctExplanation: False. mRNA is a temporary work order read in the cytoplasm, then shredded — no nucleus entry, no integration toolkit. Cells process millions of native mRNAs the same way daily.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Genome editing needs nuclear access plus integration enzymes; vaccine mRNA has neither and degrades in days. Familiarity should calm: your cells translate and trash mRNA constantly.
lessonContent:
Mechanistic checklists dissolve scary claims fast.
Ask what machinery each step would require.
Temporary messages can't rewrite permanent archives.
Cells already handle millions of native mRNAs daily.

title: The Invincible Youth
question: Healthy young adults sometimes skip vaccines, reasoning strong bodies need no help. Youth lowers personal risk but leaves transmission chains — and rare severe outcomes — fully intact.
correctExplanation: False. 'Strong' is not 'sterile': the young still catch, carry, and occasionally crash. Skipping trades others' safety plus a personal lottery ticket for zero gain.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Low risk is not no risk, and infectiousness doesn't check gym memberships. The young vaccinate partly as couriers' quarantine — protecting grandparents through their own arms.
lessonContent:
Low risk never equals no risk or no transmission.
Strength doesn't sterilize; fitness isn't quarantine.
Others' safety rides partly on young arms.
Lottery tickets hide inside 'never happens to me'.

title: The Trained Tolerance
question: The hygiene hypothesis proposes that diverse microbial exposure in childhood calibrates immunity, and its absence may tilt systems toward allergy and autoimmunity.
correctExplanation: True — with nuance. Farm-child and microbiome studies support calibration-by-exposure; the hypothesis guides research, not dirt-eating prescriptions. Training data shapes immune judgment.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Systems learn self-from-other partly through early microbial curricula — thin training data, jumpier classifiers. Note the boundary: exposure science, not an excuse to abandon sanitation.
lessonContent:
Classifiers need training data, immune ones included.
Thin curricula produce jumpier judgments.
Hypotheses guide research, not prescriptions.
Support has limits — sanitation still saves millions.

title: The Antibacterial Edge
question: Antibacterial soaps clean hands better than plain soap for everyday health. Trials find no added benefit, while the additives raise resistance and irritation concerns.
correctExplanation: False. Plain soap's mechanical removal does the work; antibacterial extras add marketing, not medicine — plus resistance selection. Technique beats chemistry at the sink.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Twenty-second scrubbing removes microbes physically; triclosan-style additives show no everyday edge and may breed resistance. Regulators agreed: marketing outran evidence.
lessonContent:
Mechanical removal does the sink's real work.
Additives need proof, not just prefixes.
Resistance can be selected at bathroom sinks.
Technique (twenty seconds) beats chemistry.

title: The Once Is Enough
question: After suffering one cold, people sometimes assume immunity to all future colds. Hundreds of rhinoviruses plus mutating strains make each cold a narrow, temporary shield.
correctExplanation: False. Immunity covers the culprit strain, not the hundred-plus cousins queuing behind it. One cold is one narrow lesson in a vast curriculum.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Rhinovirus diversity plus constant mutation means last month's shield rarely fits next month's invader. 'A cold' is a hundred diseases sharing a waiting room.
lessonContent:
Diversity defeats single-dose experience.
Narrow shields fail against cousin armies.
'A cold' is a hundred diseases in a trench coat.
Temporary, strain-specific: read immunity's fine print.
Share this: blame rhinovirus diversity for your next sniffle.

title: The Stressed Shield
question: Chronic stress measurably weakens immune defenses — slowing wound healing and dulling vaccine responses — through sustained stress-hormone signaling.
correctExplanation: True. Caregiver and exam-season studies show suppressed immunity under prolonged strain. Acute stress can briefly mobilize; chronic stress taxes and depletes.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Cortisol's long simmer redirects resources from defense to endurance — wounds linger, vaccines underperform. Duration flips stress from spur to suppressant.
lessonContent:
Duration flips stress from spur to suppressant.
Hormones reallocate defense budgets under strain.
Wounds and vaccines both grade chronic pressure.
Recovery, not endurance, restores the shield.
Share this: prescribe rest as immune medicine once.

title: The Endless Training
question: If moderate exercise supports immunity, then ever-heavier training must strengthen it further without limit.
correctExplanation: False. The curve bends: moderate training boosts, but extreme overtraining opens an infection window (marathon sniffles are classic). Dose makes the medicine — and the poison.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Immunity follows a J-curve with exercise: couch and ultramarathon both raise sick days, moderation minimizes them. More is better until suddenly it isn't.
lessonContent:
J-curves hide where straight lines are assumed.
Dose decides medicine versus poison.
Moderation minimizes what extremes maximize.
'U-shaped' thinking beats 'more is better'.

title: The Autism Link
question: A 1998 paper linked a childhood vaccine to autism; later investigations exposed falsified data, the paper was retracted, and million-child studies found no link.
correctExplanation: True. Fraud, retraction, then massive nulls — the full arc. Timing coincidences (diagnosis age overlaps vaccine schedules) keep the scare shambling without evidence.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Wakefield's fabrication collapsed under inquiry, and epidemiology at million-child scale confirmed nothing. Retraction ends the paper; only repetition ends the rumor.
lessonContent:
Fraud plus timing coincidence outlives retraction.
Million-child nulls outweigh one faked dozen.
Retraction ends papers, not rumors — repeat corrections.
Overlapping schedules manufacture false blame.

title: The Borrowed Guard
question: Newborns arrive with a starter set of maternal antibodies that guard early weeks before fading, which is partly why some vaccines wait for later months.
correctExplanation: True. Placental IgG loans protection that decays over months — a bridge to the infant's own immunity. Schedules time doses for when the loan expires.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Mother's antibodies patrol the newborn temporarily, even blunting some early vaccines — hence the calendar's careful timing. Borrowed guards hold the fort until recruits train.
lessonContent:
Borrowed protection bridges to self-sufficiency.
Loans expire on schedule — time doses accordingly.
Maternal gifts can blunt early shots (by design).
Calendars encode decay curves, not bureaucracy.

title: The Milk Patrol
question: Breast milk delivers living immune factors — antibodies, white cells, and prebiotics — that actively protect nursing infants' guts and airways.
correctExplanation: True. Milk is immune logistics: secretory IgA paints mucosa, leukocytes patrol, oligosaccharides feed good microbes. Food plus force in one package.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Beyond nutrition, milk deploys an immune convoy — antibodies coating linings, cells on patrol, prebiotics provisioning allies. Evolution ships defense with dinner.
lessonContent:
Food can double as force deployment.
Mucosal painting, patrols, provisioning — layered defense.
Evolution ships defense with dinner.
Logistics thinking reveals milk's second job.

title: The Sleeping Virus
question: Shingles erupts when the chickenpox virus, dormant in nerve roots for decades, reactivates — which is why only people who had chickenpox (or the live vaccine) risk it.
correctExplanation: True. Varicella never truly leaves; it sleeps in ganglia until immunity wanes with age or stress. Shingles is chickenpox's second act, decades later.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Latency explains the delay: the virus waits out decades in nerve tissue, then encores when surveillance slips. Adult shingles vaccination exists precisely because dormancy ends.
lessonContent:
Latency lets viruses outwait decades.
Dormancy ends when surveillance slips.
Second acts follow first infections faithfully.
Nerve tissue harbors history, not just signals.
Share this: explain shingles as chickenpox's encore.

title: The Twenty Seconds
question: Thorough handwashing measurably cuts respiratory infections, because soap dismantles viral envelopes and scrubbing removes what soap loosens.
correctExplanation: True. Trials show real drops in colds and flu from hand hygiene — chemistry plus mechanics, twenty seconds. The cheapest clinical trial ever keeps replicating.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Enveloped viruses fall apart in surfactants, and friction evicts the rest. No hype, no additives needed — technique and time deliver the effect.
lessonContent:
Chemistry plus mechanics beats either alone.
Envelopes dissolve; friction evicts.
Twenty seconds is a dose, not a suggestion.
Cheapest interventions replicate most reliably.
